headings.title: Introduction to Maternal Physiology in Pregnancy
headings.content: Pregnancy is a profound physiological journey characterized by remarkable anatomical, biochemical, and systemic adaptations across nearly every organ system in the maternal body. For student nurses preparing for clinical practice and board examinations in Nigeria, understanding these changes is vital. These physiological adjustments serve two primary purposes: to nurture the growing fetus and to prepare the maternal body for the immense physical demands of labor, delivery, and subsequent lactation. Most of these profound transformations are triggered and sustained by hormonal signals, primarily human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), estrogen, progesterone, and human placental lactogen (hPL), which are secreted by the developing conceptus and placenta. As a nurse, distinguishing between normal physiological variants of pregnancy and true pathological states is essential for providing safe, holistic, and evidence-based antenatal care. For instance, an increase in blood volume or a mild systolic heart murmur is typically expected, whereas severe hypertension or proteinuria signals pathology such as pre-eclampsia. By grasping the baseline physiology, nurses can effectively monitor maternal-fetal well-being, anticipate potential complications, and deliver targeted health education that empowers pregnant women to navigate their bodily changes with confidence. Throughout this module, we will explore the intricate adaptations of the cardiovascular, respiratory, renal, gastrointestinal, endocrine, musculoskeletal, and integumentary systems, equipping you with the critical knowledge needed to excel in maternal and child health nursing.

headings.title: Cardiovascular and Hemodynamic Adaptations
headings.content: The cardiovascular system undergoes dramatic adaptations during pregnancy to accommodate the metabolic demands of the growing fetus and the low-resistance uteroplacental unit. One of the most significant changes is the expansion of maternal blood volume, which increases by approximately 40% to 50% above non-pregnant levels, largely driven by a rise in plasma volume that outpaces red blood cell production. This disproportionate increase leads to physiological 'dilutional anemia' of pregnancy, characterized by a normal drop in hemoglobin and hematocrit concentrations. Cardiac output rises significantly by 30% to 50%, achieved primarily through an increase in stroke volume and a moderate rise in heart rate by about 15 to 20 beats per minute. Concurrently, systemic vascular resistance decreases due to the smooth muscle-relaxing effects of progesterone on blood vessels, causing maternal blood pressure to drop during the first and second trimesters before returning near baseline by term. Anatomically, the enlarging uterus displaces the heart upward and to the left, which can alter the point of maximal impulse and occasionally produce innocent systolic murmurs. Furthermore, as pregnancy progresses, the gravid uterus can compress the inferior vena cava and descending aorta when the woman lies supine, leading to supine hypotensive syndrome—characterized by dizziness, pallor, and hypotension. Nurses must educate pregnant clients to rest in a lateral recumbent position, preferably on the left side, to optimize venous return and maintain adequate uteroplacental perfusion.

headings.title: Respiratory System Alterations and Gas Exchange
headings.content: Respiratory system alterations occur primarily to meet the increased oxygen consumption requirements of the mother and fetus, as well as to facilitate the elimination of fetal carbon dioxide. As the uterus enlarges, it exerts upward pressure on the diaphragm, elevating it by up to 4 centimeters. Despite this physical restriction, the thoracic cage changes shape, with the subcostal angle widening and the transverse diameter of the chest expanding to compensate. Tidal volume—the amount of air inhaled and exhaled with each breath—increases significantly by about 30% to 40%. This increase is largely mediated by progesterone, which acts on the respiratory center in the brainstem to increase the sensitivity of the respiratory center to carbon dioxide. Consequently, the respiratory rate remains relatively unchanged or only slightly increased, but minute ventilation rises markedly. This hyperventilation state leads to a physiological mild respiratory alkalosis, which is compensated for by the kidneys excreting bicarbonate, creating a favorable gradient for carbon dioxide to diffuse across the placenta from the fetus to the mother. Additionally, pregnancy induces mucosal edema and capillary congestion throughout the upper respiratory tract due to elevated estrogen levels, frequently resulting in complaints of nasal stuffiness, epistaxis, and voice changes. Student nurses must recognize these symptoms as normal pregnancy variants rather than acute upper respiratory infections.

headings.title: Renal and Urinary Tract Modifications
headings.content: The renal and urinary systems undergo profound anatomical and functional changes to manage the increased metabolic waste products of both the mother and the developing fetus. Anatomically, high levels of progesterone cause relaxation of smooth muscle throughout the urinary tract, leading to dilation of the renal pelves and ureters (a condition known as physiological hydroureter and hydronephrosis, more pronounced on the right side due to dextrorotation of the uterus). This urinary stasis, combined with the compression of the ureters by the pelvic brim and gravid uterus, creates an environment highly favorable for bacterial growth, significantly increasing the risk of asymptomatic bacteriuria and acute pyelonephritis. Functionally, renal plasma flow and glomerular filtration rate (GFR) increase dramatically by up to 50% early in the first trimester and remain elevated until term. Because of this increased GFR, serum levels of waste products such as creatinine and urea are normally decreased in pregnancy, so values that would be considered 'normal' in a non-pregnant state may actually indicate renal impairment in an expectant mother. Furthermore, increased GFR often exceeds the renal tubules' capacity to reabsorb glucose and proteins, leading to mild, benign gestational glucosuria and trace proteinuria. During routine antenatal visits, nurses must diligently screen urine samples while understanding that trace protein and glucose can occasionally be normal variants, though persistent or high levels warrant immediate diagnostic workup for gestational hypertension or gestational diabetes.

headings.title: Gastrointestinal and Metabolic Adjustments
headings.content: Gastrointestinal adaptations during pregnancy are extensive and directly impact the comfort and nutrition of the expectant mother. High circulating levels of progesterone relax the smooth muscle tissue of the entire gastrointestinal tract, leading to decreased gastric motility, delayed gastric emptying, and reduced lower esophageal sphincter tone. These changes frequently result in common pregnancy discomforts such as heartburn (pyrosis), acid reflux, bloating, and constipation. Constipation is further exacerbated by the mechanical compression of the large intestines by the growing uterus and increased water absorption from the colon. Nausea and vomiting, particularly during the first trimester, are classic symptoms often linked to rising levels of hCG and estrogen. Additionally, increased blood flow and estrogen levels frequently cause gingival hyperemia, rendering the gums soft, spongy, and prone to bleeding during brushing—a condition known as pregnancy gingivitis. Metabolically, pregnancy is characterized by a shift toward an anabolic state in early gestation (fat storage) and a catabolic state in late gestation (ensuring continuous glucose supply to the fetus). Fasting hypoglycemia and postprandial hyperglycemia can occur, mediated by human placental lactogen (hPL), which induces peripheral insulin resistance to ensure ample glucose availability for fetal growth. Nurses play a crucial role in managing these symptoms by advising small, frequent meals, maintaining adequate hydration, encouraging high-fiber diets, and promoting meticulous dental hygiene.

headings.title: Endocrine and Hormonal Shifts
headings.content: The endocrine system undergoes monumental shifts during pregnancy, transforming the placenta into a temporary yet powerful endocrine organ that secretes numerous hormones essential for maintaining the gestation. Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) is the earliest placental hormone produced, signaling the corpus luteum to continue producing progesterone during early pregnancy until the placenta is fully developed to take over steroidogenesis. Estrogen and progesterone levels rise steadily throughout gestation; estrogen stimulates the growth of uterine muscle and breast tissue, while progesterone maintains the uterine lining, suppresses uterine contractility, and relaxes smooth muscle throughout the body. Another vital placental hormone, human placental lactogen (hPL), acts as an antagonist to maternal insulin, ensuring adequate glucose availability for fetal nutrition while promoting maternal lipolysis. Furthermore, the maternal pituitary gland enlarges by approximately 130% due to hyperplasia and hypertrophy of estrogen-stimulated prolactin-secreting cells, leading to markedly elevated prolactin levels to prepare the breasts for lactation, even though high estrogen and progesterone levels inhibit milk production until after delivery. The thyroid gland also undergoes physiological enlargement and increased activity, with rises in thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG) and total T3 and T4, though free thyroid hormone levels remain generally within the normal non-pregnant range. Nurses must understand these complex hormonal cascades to interpret laboratory results correctly and educate clients on normal versus abnormal endocrine findings.

headings.title: Musculoskeletal and Dermatological Changes
headings.content: Musculoskeletal and dermatological alterations during pregnancy are largely driven by hormonal loosening of connective tissue and the mechanical shift in the mother's center of gravity. The hormone relaxin, along with progesterone, causes significant relaxation of the pelvic ligaments and joints (such as the pubic symphysis and sacroiliac joints) to facilitate passage of the fetus through the birth canal during delivery. This ligamentous laxity, combined with the anterior displacement of the uterus, alters the woman's posture, leading to a pronounced lumbar lordosis often referred to as the 'waddle' of pregnancy. This postural shift frequently results in backache, pelvic girdle pain, and occasional numbness or tingling in the arms due to traction on the brachial plexus. Dermatologically, increased levels of melanocyte-stimulating hormone (MSH), estrogen, and progesterone lead to hyperpigmentation in many areas of the body. Common manifestations include the lineament nigra (a dark vertical line down the midline of the abdomen), chloasma or melasma (the 'mask of pregnancy' on the face), and darkening of the areolae and vulva. Additionally, stretched connective tissue in the dermis often results in striae gravidarum (stretch marks) over the abdomen, breasts, and thighs. Elevated estrogen levels can also trigger vascular changes, manifesting as palmar erythema and spider angiomas. Nurses should educate clients that while these musculoskeletal and skin changes are largely normal and self-limiting, proper body mechanics, supportive belts, and gentle exercises can significantly alleviate discomfort.

headings.title: Nursing Assessment and Patient Education
headings.content: Comprehensive nursing assessment and patient education are the cornerstones of effective antenatal care, requiring a thorough understanding of physiological changes in pregnancy. Nurses must conduct systematic head-to-toe assessments during every antenatal visit, paying close attention to vital signs, weight gain patterns, fundal height progression, and signs of potential complications. Education must be individualized, culturally sensitive, and tailored to the gestational age of the fetus. For instance, in the first trimester, nurses should educate women on managing nausea, vomiting, and fatigue while emphasizing the critical importance of avoiding teratogens, smoking, and alcohol. During the second and third trimesters, education shifts toward preparing for fetal movement monitoring, recognizing warning signs of preterm labor, understanding expected discomforts like backache and heartburn, and discussing safe relief measures. Crucially, nurses must teach pregnant clients to identify 'red flag' symptoms that require immediate reporting to a healthcare provider, such as severe headache, visual disturbances, sudden facial or hand edema, vaginal bleeding, fluid leakage, and decreased fetal movement. By empowering expectant mothers with clear, evidence-based knowledge and compassionate support, nurses help bridge the gap between clinical theory and practical self-care, ultimately promoting optimal maternal-fetal outcomes across Nigeria and beyond.
